covers.quote: Use protective markings for government information.
There are 4 levels of security classification – ‘Official: Sensitive’, ‘Protected’, ‘Secret’ and ‘Top Secret’.
‘Official’ and ‘Unofficial’ are not security classifications and are not mandatory markings.

rules.quote: All security-classified information, including emails, must carry protective markings.
rules.violation_condition: Security-classified government information lacks a protective marking.
when: Applies to security-classified information, including emails and information metadata.
The security classifications are Official: Sensitive, Protected, Secret and Top Secret.
Official and Unofficial are not security classifications, and those markings are not mandatory.
Information management markers are optional.
rules.why: G-2 combines the information types subject to the same missing-marking check; G-3 preserves the optional markings as exceptions.

rules.quote: Caveat markings are mandatory for security classifications of Protected or higher.
rules.violation_condition: Information classified Protected, Secret or Top Secret lacks a caveat marking.
when: Applies to information classified Protected, Secret or Top Secret.
rules.why: The grain test distinguishes a missing caveat from a missing security-classification marking.

covers.quote: To achieve clearly identifiable protective markings, the PSPF recommends:

rules.violation_condition: An applied protective marking contains lowercase letters.
when: Applies to protective markings themselves, not references to their names in general content.
This is a PSPF formatting recommendation.
rules.why: The grain test separates capitalisation from the independently checkable formatting recommendations.

rules.violation_condition: An applied protective marking is not formatted in bold.
when: Applies to protective markings themselves, not references to their names in general content.
This is a PSPF formatting recommendation.
rules.why: The grain test treats missing bold formatting as independent of case, size and colour.

rules.specification: The page supplies neither a minimum font size nor a comparison that defines ‘large’. A size criterion must be resolved before this check can reliably produce findings.
rules.violation_condition: An applied protective marking is set in a font size that does not qualify as large.
when: Applies to protective markings themselves, not references to their names in general content.
This is a PSPF formatting recommendation.
rules.why: The grain test separates font size from other formatting; E-4 prevents inventing a size threshold.

rules.specification: The page does not define how to determine whether a colour is distinctive, or specify a palette or contrast criterion.
rules.violation_condition: An applied protective marking uses a colour that does not make it visually distinctive.
when: Applies to protective markings themselves, not references to their names in general content.
This is a PSPF formatting recommendation.
rules.why: The grain test separates visual distinctiveness from the preference for a particular colour; E-4 prevents inventing a contrast threshold.

rules.violation_condition: An applied protective marking uses a colour other than red.
when: Applies to protective markings themselves, not references to their names in general content.
Red is preferred, not mandatory.
rules.why: The grain test distinguishes the explicit preference for red from the separate recommendation for a distinctive colour.

rules.quote: placing markings at the centre top and bottom of each page
rules.violation_condition: A page carrying security-classified information lacks a protective marking centred at its top or at its bottom.
when: Applies to the placement of protective markings on pages.
This is a PSPF formatting recommendation.
rules.why: G-2 keeps the required top-and-bottom occurrences together as one marking-placement check.

rules.quote: separating markings by a double forward slash to help clearly differentiate each marking.
rules.violation_condition: Successive protective markings are not separated by a double forward slash.
when: Applies when multiple protective markings appear together.
This is a PSPF formatting recommendation.
rules.why: The grain test identifies one independently checkable separator requirement.

covers.quote: In general content, use an initial capital unless you are reporting how the protective marking actually appears on the page.
write the marking as it appears

parts.quote: Only those with an existing Negative Vetting 1 security clearance are considered for supervised temporary access to Top Secret information.
The field report was stamped ‘TOP SECRET’.

rules.quote: Use initial capitals to write about protective markings
rules.violation_condition: A protective marking named in general content is written without initial capitals, or a reported marking's capitalisation differs from its actual appearance.
when: Use initial capitals for references to protective markings in general content.
When reporting how a marking actually appears on a page, preserve its actual capitalisation instead.
Checking the reporting exception requires access to the marking being reported.
rules.why: G-4 absorbs the body's restatement; G-2 treats reporting the actual appearance as a case of the same capitalisation check.

parts.quote: The field report was stamped ‘TOP SECRET’.

rules.violation_condition: A protective marking reported as it actually appears on a page is not enclosed in quotation marks.
when: Applies when reporting how a protective marking actually appears on a page.
rules.why: The grain test separates missing quotation marks from incorrect capitalisation.
